scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Faroese chain dance is a medieval dance form preserved in the Faroe Islands, where it remains a living tradition.
It is closely linked to the singing of kvæði, traditional Faroese ballads that tell stories of heroes and history.
Historically, the dance was not performed during Lent, a practice believed to date back to the Catholic Middle Ages.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Faroese chain dance is a communal folk tradition practiced mainly during the dark winter months, from September or October until Lent.
It is traditionally not danced during Lent, reflecting historical religious customs.
The dance is central to social gatherings and cultural celebrations, including the national holiday Ólavsøka, where thousands participate in the midnight dance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a continuous circle holding hands, with the right hand overlapping the left hand of the neighbor.

The basic step, stígingarstev, involves six rhythmic foot movements to the left: left foot steps forward left, right foot steps to left, left foot steps forward left, right foot follows, right foot steps sideways or backward, left foot follows.
This pattern repeats steadily to the ballad's rhythm.
Watch for Stígingarstev, Trokingarstev, Bandadansur.

Formation: Continuous circle or multiple concentric circles; dancers follow chain's curves, passing face-to-face twice per round

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied solely by singing of kvæði, Faroese ballads performed a cappella without instrumental accompaniment.
The ballads are sung by a lead singer called the skipari, who knows all verses, while the dancers join in at the chorus.
The pulse is six-bar phrases.
A cappella ballad singing with steady, rhythmic foot stamping providing a percussive pulse; the voice leads the melody with communal chorus responses.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance is traditionally performed indoors during the dark winter months, from autumn until the start of Lent, often in community halls or private gatherings.
At large events like Ólavsøka, the national holiday, the dance takes place outdoors late at night.
There is no specific costume mandated, but dancers often wear traditional or everyday clothing suitable for communal folk dancing.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The skipari, or lead singer, is a central figure in the dance, responsible for knowing and singing all verses of the kvæði.

Several Faroese dance associations have been instrumental in preserving and promoting the dance, including Tvøroyrar Dansifelag (founded 1983, originally 1958), Sumbiar Dansifelag (1966), and Dansifelagið í Havn (1952).

Three main variants exist: the common stígingarstev, characterized by slow leftward stepping; the trokingarstev, where dancers stand mostly still or move backward during verses and step forward during refrains, more common in southern islands like Suðuroy; and the bandadansur or ribbon dance, involving two rows holding ribbons and passing under raised ribbons during refrains.
The Faroese chain dance is a direct descendant of medieval circle dances, preserved uniquely in the Faroe Islands.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Faroese chain dance is shares region of Danish folk dance: Both are Nordic folk dances with circle formations, but Faroese chain dance uniquely uses only vocal ballads without instruments.

visual_brief.setting_notes: The Faroese chain dance is a communal folk tradition practiced mainly during the dark winter months, from September or October until Lent. It is traditionally not danced during Lent, reflecting historical religious customs. The dance is central to social gatherings and cultural celebrations, including the national holiday Ólavsøka, where thousands participate in the midnight dance. The dance expresses the narrative of Faroese ballads, with dancers physically embodying emotions and events described in the songs. It serves as a living link to Faroese history and identity.
